adopt.title: Adopting {name}
adopt.stepsLabel: How to take a stray dog home
adopt.step1Body:
Offer the dog some food, such as sausage or kibble. Observe its behaviour to determine if it wants to interact with you.

Positive signs: approaches you, takes food from your hand, stands calmly while eating, looks at your face, sits down and eats peacefully, jumps around happily, stands up on its hind legs, or barks in a friendly manner.

Negative signs: backs away, turns away, cringes, runs a short distance away, flees, growls, avoids eye contact, presses against a wall, or ignores the food.

If you establish positive contact, move on to step two. If the reaction is negative, assess how urgently the dog needs to leave the street. Not urgent: try to find a common language over 10–15 days, gradually building trust. Urgent: seek help from canine behaviourists, rescue activists, or volunteers.
adopt.step2Body: Feed the dog every day. It is best to use the same food you plan to feed it at home. Buy a well-fitting collar and put it on the dog's neck. Do not try to walk the dog on a leash right away — that might scare it.
adopt.step3Body: Give the dog a name and call it by its name. Use happy, encouraging tones when calling it over. Place the food in a dog bowl right in front of you.
adopt.step4Body:
If the dog has been living in one place for a long time (on the street or in a yard), consult a veterinarian. Before bringing the dog home, make sure to get the necessary vaccinations and treat it for parasites.

Important: check the weather forecast before vaccination. Shots should be administered during favourable weather conditions, without sudden turnarounds (such as continuous rain or severe frost) during the post-vaccination period — meaning the following 10 days.
adopt.step5Body: If the dog lives near you, try inviting it into your home. Do not rush the process; it may take some time.
adopt.step6Body: Purchase all the necessary dog supplies in advance: dog shampoo, a separate towel, food, a bed or sleeping mat, treats, toys, and absorbent pee pads.
adopt.step7Body: Bring the dog home. Give it a bath, feed it, and begin adapting it to the home environment while gradually training it to use a leash.
adopt.step8Body:
Take your pet to a veterinary clinic and run routine blood tests to ensure there are no hidden infections.

In case of any difficulties, always reach out to professionals: canine behaviourists, veterinarians, animal welfare activists, or groomers.
adopt.docsBody:
· Passport (yours)
· Vet certificate from the clinic
· Vaccination booklet with rabies dated within the last year
· Microchip registration in your name
· For international travel: EU pet passport (issued by the clinic) and a 30-day waiting period after rabies vaccination

tour.promptTitle: Welcome to The Street Dog App
tour.promptBody: A quick 3-step tour to show you how everything fits together. Takes about a minute.
tour.step1Body: Every logged sighting bumps your XP. Brand-new dogs and new-to-you dogs earn more, and each 100 XP is a new researcher level. Tap the card to expand your achievements.
tour.step2Body: Pick a walkable chunk and find 5 dogs for +100 XP, or grab the daily 'one dog a day' directive for a quick +15 XP. You'll find them in the Missions tab.
tour.step3Body: Switch between every dog nearby, ones you found first, ones you've logged, and your favourites. Ready to start?

partnerClinics.firstAidTitle: What to do if you encounter a sick or injured dog
partnerClinics.firstAidBody:
Determine the severity of the condition:

1. The dog is injured: the wound is old or fresh, or the dog is bleeding.
2. The dog is unwell: the animal is not moving, does not respond to calls, is shivering, or is whimpering / howling.
3. The dog is limping: it is holding up or dragging its paw, the paw is bleeding, or there is an open fracture.
4. The dog was in an accident (car hit): it is lying down and whimpering, limping, lying down and unable to get up, or clearly injured.
5. The dog looks sick: it has hair loss, visible wounds, severe emaciation, or is vomiting.
6. The dog is trapped: it is stuck in a fence, tangled in a rope, wire, or netting, or caught in a trap.

Providing assistance:

When providing emergency aid, first assess the dog from a safe distance. Be careful to avoid getting bitten by the animal.

Your action plan:
· Take photos and videos of the animal.
· Call a veterinary clinic to consult with a doctor or write to their support chat.
· Call a specialized animal ambulance service.
· Ask volunteers and animal rights activists for help.
· Try to transport the dog to a clinic yourself or wait for help to arrive on-site.

partnerOrgs.intro: Dog welfare in Tbilisi runs through a small set of organisations. If a dog needs capture, shelter, treatment, or rehoming, these are the people to call.
partnerOrgs.org1Mission: Controls Tbilisi's stray animal population and ensures public safety. Responds to 112 reports, captures aggressive or vulnerable strays, runs the municipal shelter, and handles vaccination, sterilization, microchipping, and pet registration.
partnerOrgs.org1Note: Call 112 to report aggressive or vulnerable strays
partnerOrgs.org2Mission: Rescues and treats severely injured dogs from across Georgia, places them with families locally and abroad (especially Germany), and advocates against cruelty in state-run shelters. "Give a dog a second chance."
partnerOrgs.org2Note: Treatment · international adoption · animal rights advocacy

support.title: Help us keep building
support.intro: The Street Dog App is a volunteer-run citizen-science project. Every sighting you log, every dog you name, and every share with a friend grows the open dataset on Tbilisi's free-roaming dogs.
support.contactBody: Reach out for support, partnership, NGO collaboration, data access, press, or just to say hi. We read everything that comes in.
support.donateBody: We're setting up direct donation channels. In the meantime, drop us a line and we'll share the best way to support the work financially — from one-off contributions to clinic vouchers for street dogs.
support.collabBody:
Open to: vet clinics, rescue networks, university research groups, dog welfare NGOs, mapping & data-viz volunteers, photographers, and translators.

We share aggregated data with research groups and shelters. Reach out about data partnerships, custom dashboards, or starting a local chapter in your city.
support.helpInPlaceBody: Walk through your neighbourhood and log a dog. Add a name. Flag a health issue. The dataset gets richer every time.
